strengths: Solid theoretical foundation: the paper derives a sufficient-and-necessary condition (Thm 3.2) for the optimal low-rank update via truncated SVD of the gradient, then provides two tractable closed-form relaxations (scalar scaling in Thm 3.5, column-wise scaling in Thm 3.7) that avoid both the SVD cost and the need to reset adaptive-optimizer moment estimators, which is a genuine technical advance over ReLoRA (restart-based) and connects LoRA-GA as a special case.

The method is well motivated by concrete, previously identified shortcomings of high-rank LoRA variants (ReLoRA's restart overhead, MoRA's ad-hoc nonlinear compression, HiRA's O(mn) memory cost from Hadamard backprop), and the paper offers a clear complexity/memory analysis showing ScaLoRA(-I) compares favorably.

Extensive empirical validation across model scales (184M DeBERTaV3 to 12B Gemma-3) and task families (GLUE, 8 commonsense reasoning datasets, MetaMath/GSM8K/MATH), with consistent (if sometimes modest) improvements over LoRA, MoRA, HiRA, ReLoRA, and LoRA-GA.

Careful ablations and diagnostics: verification of the rank(∇ℓ)≥2r assumption, empirical rate of positivity for the linear system in Thm 3.7, rank/stable-rank analysis of accumulated updates versus baselines, ablation on interval I, and scalar-only vs. column-wise scaling ablation, all of which help substantiate the theoretical claims with empirical evidence.
Reasonably transparent discussion of limitations (storage overhead, escalated per-step compute cost relative to LoRA) and a mitigation strategy (ScaLoRA-I) with a reported time/memory trade-off.
weaknesses: The globally optimal column-wise scaling (Thm 3.7) only applies when a 2r×2r linear system yields a non-negative solution, which the authors report holds in roughly 80% of layers/iterations; the remaining cases fall back to a different (scalar) scheme with no formal justification that the resulting mixture strategy retains any global optimality guarantee, somewhat undercutting the 'rigorous performance guarantees' framing in the abstract.

The core derivation relies on minimizing a majorizing quadratic upper bound of the loss (via the L-smoothness assumption) rather than the true loss; while common in optimization, the connection between minimizing this per-step surrogate and actual downstream task performance is asserted rather than rigorously established, and L is treated as a tuned hyperparameter, weakening the 'optimal' terminology used throughout.

The performance gains over strong high-rank baselines (HiRA, MoRA, LoRA-GA) are frequently small (e.g., ~0.5% average on GLUE, ~0.5-1% on commonsense reasoning) and often within one standard deviation of the reported error bars, raising questions about the practical significance of the improvement despite the added complexity.

Per-step time complexity O(mnr) is of the same order as the low-rank forward/backward pass itself, and Figure 3 shows ScaLoRA incurs 50%+ additional wall-clock time versus LoRA without the -I variant; while ScaLoRA-I amortizes this, its benefit is empirically tied to the (largely heuristic) choice of interval I, and the ablation (Table 10) shows a noticeable accuracy/loss trade-off as I grows.

ScaLoRA requires storing the full merged weight matrix per layer rather than only the small adapters, which the paper dismisses as inconsequential due to abundant disk space, but this changes the deployment/multi-tenant story that makes LoRA attractive in the first place (e.g., swapping/stacking many lightweight adapters), and this trade-off is not empirically explored.

Some relevant recent baselines mentioned in related work (e.g., DoRA, PiSSA, AdaLoRA-style budget allocation) are not included in the main experimental comparisons, and MoRA/HiRA are dropped from the largest-scale (12B) experiments due to scalability limits, leaving the strongest baselines untested at the largest model size where the method's practical value would be most impactful.

strengths: Genuine theoretical contribution: Theorem 3.2 establishes a sufficient and necessary condition for the per-step optimal low-rank adapter (connecting it to truncated SVD of the gradient), and Theorems 3.5/3.7 derive closed-form optimal scalar and column-wise scaling factors, which is a non-trivial analytical result (detailed, careful proofs provided in the appendix).

The core idea of merging the current adapter into the frozen weight and refactoring a new low-rank direction elegantly sidesteps the telescoping-sum limitation of vanilla LoRA while, via Lemmas 3.3/3.6, allowing AdamW moment estimators to be updated in closed form without restart/re-warmup, addressing a concrete weakness of ReLoRA.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning model scales from 184M (DeBERTaV3) to 12B (Gemma-3) and task types (GLUE NLU, 8 commonsense reasoning benchmarks, math reasoning with GSM8K/MATH), with consistent (if often modest) improvements over LoRA, MoRA, HiRA, ReLoRA, and LoRA-GA.

Thoughtful diagnostic experiments: rank/stable-rank growth analysis (Table 3), validation of the theoretical assumptions (Fig 2c/2d), overhead comparison (Fig 3, Table 5), and ablations on the intermittent variant ScaLoRA-I and on scalar vs. column scaling, which substantiate the mechanism behind the claimed gains rather than just reporting end accuracy.

Honest treatment of limitations (extra time/space overhead of full ScaLoRA, storage of the merged weight matrix, conditions under which the closed-form column scaling is not guaranteed feasible) rather than hiding them.
weaknesses: The reported performance gains are frequently small and close to the reported standard deviations (e.g., GLUE average 88.98 vs. HiRA 88.46 vs. LoRA 88.13 with only 3 runs; LLaMA3-8B commonsense average 77.85 vs. HiRA 77.46 vs. LoRA 76.83), making it hard to be fully confident the improvements are not within noise, especially since no significance tests are reported.

The theory rests on a global Lipschitz-smoothness surrogate (Assumption 3.1) with constant L treated purely as a tunable hyperparameter rather than estimated, and the per-step optimal-scaling derivation assumes plain GD, while the actual optimizer used in experiments is AdamW; the translation from the GD-based optimality theory to the adaptive-optimizer implementation is heuristic rather than rigorously justified, somewhat weakening the 'rigorous performance guarantees' claim made in the abstract.

The applicability of the headline closed-form results is conditional and not always satisfied: Theorem 3.2 requires rank(∇ℓ(W_t)) ≥ 2r and Theorem 3.7's column-wise scaling requires a non-negative solution to a 2r×2r linear system, which the paper's own Figure 2d shows holds only ~80% of the time, so the method frequently falls back to the less expressive scalar-scaling scheme via an ad hoc feasibility check rather than a jointly optimal selection rule.

ScaLoRA incurs substantial additional computational cost (50%+ runtime over LoRA per Figure 3) comparable to or exceeding MoRA/HiRA; the proposed amortized fix (ScaLoRA-I) only partially alleviates this and further weakens the connection between the proven per-step optimality and what is actually run in practice (optimal scaling is only approximately valid between the I-step intervals).

Some comparisons are incomplete: MoRA and HiRA are dropped from the largest-scale (12B) math experiments due to scalability concerns, so the paper cannot show ScaLoRA actually outperforms its strongest baselines at the scale most relevant to practical LLM fine-tuning; similarly, newer strong baselines mentioned in related work (DoRA, PiSSA, LoRA-pro, LoRA-RITE) are not included as empirical baselines.

The storage limitation (needing to persist the full merged W_t rather than just low-rank factors) is dismissed briefly as a non-issue due to abundant disk space, without discussing I/O overhead or practical implications for checkpointing/sharding in distributed training of very large models.

strengths: Rigorous theoretical development: necessary-and-sufficient conditions for the optimal low-rank adapter under a quadratic loss surrogate (Thm 3.2), and closed-form or efficiently-solvable optimal scaling factors for scalar (Thm 3.5) and column-wise (Thm 3.7) transforms, with full proofs provided in the appendix.

The core technical insight—restricting the new adapter to a structured transform (scaling) of the existing one—elegantly solves the practical problem of re-estimating Adam/AdamW moment statistics without restarting optimization, directly addressing a known weakness of ReLoRA.

Thorough complexity analysis comparing ScaLoRA/ScaLoRA-I to LoRA, MoRA, and HiRA in both time and memory, supported by an intermittent variant (ScaLoRA-I) that amortizes the extra cost, keeping memory overhead negligible (demonstrated empirically in Figure 3).

Broad empirical validation spanning synthetic linear regression, GLUE (DeBERTaV3), commonsense reasoning (LLaMA2-7B/LLaMA3-8B), and math reasoning (Gemma-3-12B), showing consistent (if sometimes modest) improvements over LoRA and recent high-rank variants (MoRA, HiRA, ReLoRA, LoRA-GA).

Useful diagnostic experiments (gradient rank, rank of cumulative update, percentage of column-scaling feasibility, stable rank comparisons) that substantiate the paper's theoretical claims and provide interpretability of the method's behavior.
Ablation studies on the amortization interval I and on column- vs scalar-only scaling clarify the practical trade-offs and justify design choices.
weaknesses: Performance gains over strong baselines (LoRA-GA, HiRA, MoRA, LoRA with higher rank) are often small and within or close to reported standard deviations (e.g., GLUE average +0.5%, several commonsense reasoning datasets where ScaLoRA is not top-2), raising questions about statistical significance, especially since GLUE results use only 3 random seeds.

The theoretical optimality (Thm 3.2, 3.5, 3.7) is derived from a quadratic upper bound of the loss under a global Lipschitz constant L, which is in practice an unknown, dataset/layer-dependent hyperparameter tuned via grid search; the gap between this surrogate optimum and the true per-step loss minimizer is not empirically quantified beyond the toy linear-regression example.

The column-wise scaling (Theorem 3.7) requires a non-negativity condition on the solution of a 2r×2r linear system that is not guaranteed to hold; the ~80% satisfaction rate is reported only for one dataset (RTE) with DeBERTa, and it is unclear how this generalizes across layers, architectures, and tasks, or what performance loss results from falling back to scalar scaling.

ScaLoRA's full (non-amortized) variant incurs ~50%+ extra wall-clock time versus LoRA (Figure 3), comparable to MoRA/HiRA, undermining the claimed efficiency advantage unless the intermittent ScaLoRA-I variant is used, which itself introduces an additional hyperparameter I that trades off accuracy vs. speed (Table 10) without a principled way to select it a priori.

Unlike standard LoRA, ScaLoRA must store the entire merged weight matrix Wt rather than just compact adapters, which—while dismissed as a disk-space, not memory, concern—could still complicate deployment scenarios involving multiple adapters or serving many fine-tuned variants from a shared base model.

Evaluation is limited to likelihood-based or exact-match metrics (GLUE accuracy, multiple-choice reasoning, GSM8K/MATH exact match); there is no evaluation on open-ended generation or instruction-tuning tasks where high-rank update benefits are often most showcased in the broader LoRA-variant literature.

The method introduces additional complexity (mixture of scalar/column scaling, per-layer decision via solving a linear system, Lipschitz constant as hyperparameter) that may affect reproducibility and ease of adoption compared to simpler baselines, and the hyperparameter sensitivity of L is not analyzed.
